Stack the endpoint position into a vector p(q) = FK(q). The linear-velocity rows of the Jacobian are then the partial derivatives of p, one column per joint:

J_v = [∂p/∂q₁ ∂p/∂q₂ … ∂p/∂qₙ]

Take a planar 2-link arm with link lengths l₁ and l₂, writing c₁₂ = cos(θ₁+θ₂) and s₁₂ = sin(θ₁+θ₂):

- x = l₁c₁ + l₂c₁₂
- y = l₁s₁ + l₂s₁₂

Differentiate each entry with respect to each joint:

J_v = [ −l₁s₁ − l₂s₁₂ , −l₂s₁₂ ; l₁c₁ + l₂c₁₂ , l₂c₁₂ ]

Then ṗ = J_v q̇ follows from the chain rule.

Look at column 1. It equals ẑ × (p − O₀), which is the geometric recipe z × r. So the column is the endpoint velocity when joint 1 turns at one unit rate and everything else is frozen. Column 2 is ẑ × (p − O₁), where the moment arm runs from joint 2 to the tip. This is also your check: move one joint and see whether the tip goes where the column says. For a prismatic joint, ∂p/∂dᵢ is just the axis zᵢ₋₁.

One correction before you use this for a whole 6-DOF pose. Only the position rows are derivatives of FK. The angular rows are not ∂(orientation)/∂q. Differentiating roll-pitch-yaw gives a different matrix, the "analytical Jacobian", which has singularities of its own. The geometric Jacobian takes the angular part directly: zᵢ₋₁ for a rotary joint and 0 for a prismatic one. Angular velocities add as vectors, but orientation angles don't.

Quick check: in the 2-link example, why is column 2 not just "l₂ times something that depends only on θ₂"?
